title: MITCHELL-RILEY SYNDROME
alt_titles: DIABETES, NEONATAL, WITH PANCREATIC HYPOPLASIA, INTESTINAL ATRESIA, AND GALLBLADDER APLASIA OR HYPOPLASIA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Mitchell-Riley syndrome (MTCHRS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RFX6 gene (612659) on chromosome 6q22.1.

checks.evidence_quote: Missense, splicing or frameshift mutations in RFX6 were found in five of the six available probands (Fig. 5e)

paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal and duodenal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia (Mitchell et al., 2004). Autopsies have shown a normal-appearing exocrine pancreas with no cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin (Smith et al., 2010). Most reported patients died in infancy (Mitchell et al., 2004). Some patients with RFX6 mutations have had diabetes starting in childhood rather than the neonatal period (Sansbury et al., 2015).

checks.explanation: The authors propose autosomal recessive inheritance, though they hedge it with 'probably'.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) proposed the name Mitchell-Riley syndrome, after the two clinicians who first described it. They distinguished it from Martinez-Frias syndrome, noting that the original Martinez-Frias patients had esophageal atresia and hypospadias without diabetes and that no RFX6 mutation was found in one of them. Other authors have reported patients with neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia under the Martinez-Frias syndrome name (Martinovici et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) reported 5 infants from 3 families: 2 sib pairs, 1 of them born to consanguineous parents, and an isolated case. The infants had neonatal diabetes, a hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder. Four children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. One patient had a milder form and was surviving free of insulin. On pancreatic immunohistochemistry there were a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin at all.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) described infants with neonatal diabetes and small bowel obstruction due to bowel atresia. Some had a reduced pancreatic size, but none had exocrine enzyme deficiency. The infants also had a hypoplastic gallbladder and intractable diarrhea that did not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement. Autopsies of 2 cases were reported: their proband 1, a girl born to consanguineous parents, and case 3 of a previous report. Both showed a normal-appearing exocrine pancreas with clusters of chromogranin A-positive cells but no cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. Probands 1, 4, and 5 died in the first few months of life. Proband 2 was alive at age 4.5 years. Proband 3 was alive at age 9 years and was intermittently off insulin.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins, both aged 9 years at last report. Case 1 was a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 1.65 kg (42nd centile). She had duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum. She was hyperglycemic at 2 years of age and presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at 3 years, with low insulin and C-peptide and no islet autoantibodies. She also had gastrointestinal bleeding, gastric heterotopia in the small bowel, and an absent gallbladder, and her liver function tests were normal. Case 2 was a boy born at 34 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 1.70 kg (7th centile). He had duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. He had asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia at 5 years of age, and diabetes was diagnosed at 6 years after he presented with hyperglycemia (16.0 mmol/l); he had no islet autoantibodies. He had a history of chronic iron deficiency anemia. No structural abnormality of the hepatobiliary tract was found, and his liver function tests were always normal.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) used targeted capture and deep sequencing of the exons in the shared homozygous regions in proband 2. paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) found a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18 of the RFX6 gene, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution, in 2 Turkish double first cousins with intestinal atresia and childhood-onset diabetes. In both, it was in compound heterozygosity with R726X. The mothers were heterozygous for R866X.
